introduction-what-time-is-it-really.core: In a distributed system there's no single global clock. Each machine's clock drifts, synchronisation is imperfect and messages take variable time. That means you can't reliably order events across machines by timestamp alone, which matters for databases, logs, leases, caches and conflict resolution.

first_principles.problem: Two servers record writes with wall-clock timestamps and 'last write wins' keeps the older value.

analogy.title: Synchronising watches across a big group
analogy.story: Everyone's watch is a bit off, so 'who arrived first' by watch time can be wrong.
analogy.breaks: People can compare watches face to face; servers only exchange delayed messages.

example.title: LWW gone wrong
flow: Server A (clock +2 s fast) writes v1 at 10:00:02
Server B writes v2 later, at its 10:00:01
LWW keeps v1, the older write

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Wall clocks can invert real order.

check.q: Why is last-write-wins by wall-clock timestamp risky?
check.a: Clock skew can make a later write appear older, so newer data gets discarded.

physical-clocks-drift-and-synchronizatio.core: Quartz oscillators drift by tens of parts per million (seconds per day). NTP synchronises clocks over the network, estimating offset from round-trip times, typically to within milliseconds on LANs and tens of milliseconds over the internet, with accuracy degraded by asymmetric paths and congestion. Cloud providers offer local, highly accurate time services.

first_principles.problem: Log timestamps from different hosts disagree by seconds, making incident timelines confusing.
derivation: Use **cloud time services** (Amazon Time Sync, Google NTP).

analogy.title: Pendulum clocks in different rooms
analogy.story: Each runs slightly fast or slow, so you regularly reset them against the town hall clock.
analogy.breaks: Resetting by walking to the hall has fixed delay; network delay varies unpredictably.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Know how far off each host is.

code.text:
chronyc tracking
# System time: 0.000012345 seconds fast of NTP time
chronyc sources -v

check.a: Variable and asymmetric network delay between client and time server.

ptp-when-milliseconds-arent-good-enough.core: Precision Time Protocol (IEEE 1588) achieves sub-microsecond synchronisation using hardware timestamping in NICs and switches (boundary and transparent clocks) that measure and compensate for path delay at each hop. It's used in finance (trade timestamps), telecom and cloud databases, and some cloud providers expose PTP hardware clocks to instances.

first_principles.problem: High-frequency trading regulations require timestamps accurate to microseconds, beyond NTP.
truths: Network devices can correct delay per hop.
derivation: Use cloud **PTP hardware clocks** where offered.

analogy.title: Relay timing at every checkpoint of a race
analogy.story: Each checkpoint records exact pass times, so you can subtract travel time precisely.
analogy.breaks: Race checkpoints are fixed; network paths can change, needing continuous recalibration.

check.q: What makes PTP far more accurate than NTP?
check.a: Hardware timestamping in NICs and switches that compensates for delay at each hop.

a-quirky-problem-leap-seconds.core: Leap seconds occasionally add (or could remove) a second to UTC to match Earth's rotation, creating 23:59:60. Software that assumes 60-second minutes has crashed (2012 Linux livelocks, Cloudflare's 2017 negative duration bug). Many providers smear the leap second over hours instead, and the practice is set to be abolished by 2035.

first_principles.problem: A service computes negative durations during a leap second and crashes.
truths: Wall clocks can repeat or skip.
derivation: Use **leap smearing** (Google, AWS) consistently across fleet.

analogy.title: A clock that occasionally pauses for one extra tick
analogy.story: Anyone timing an egg by the wall clock at that moment gets confused.
analogy.breaks: Egg timers just overcook; software can crash or corrupt data.

code.text:
start := time.Now()   // Go's time.Now includes a monotonic reading
doWork()
elapsed := time.Since(start)   // uses monotonic clock → never negative

check.a: Spreading the extra leap second gradually over hours so clocks never show 23:59:60 or jump.

monotonic-clocks-vs-wall-clocks.core: Wall clocks (CLOCK_REALTIME) give the date and time and can jump forwards or backwards when NTP corrects them or an admin changes them. Monotonic clocks (CLOCK_MONOTONIC) only move forward at a steady rate from an arbitrary start, so they're right for measuring durations, timeouts and rate limits but meaningless across machines or reboots.

first_principles.problem: A timeout calculated with wall time fires early when NTP steps the clock back.
derivation: **Wall clock** for timestamps shown to humans/stored.
**Monotonic clock** for durations, timeouts, rate limiting.
Never **subtract wall times** for elapsed time.

analogy.title: A calendar versus a stopwatch
analogy.story: The calendar tells you the date (and can be corrected); the stopwatch only counts elapsed time.
analogy.breaks: Stopwatches can be shared; monotonic readings are meaningless on another machine.

code.text:
import time
deadline = time.monotonic() + 5.0
while time.monotonic() < deadline:
    if try_connect(): break
    time.sleep(0.1)

check.q: Which clock should you use to measure a request's latency?

the-need-for-logical-time.core: Often we don't need true time, just consistent ordering of events that are causally related: if A could have influenced B, A must come first. Lamport's 'happened-before' relation defines this partial order: events in one process are ordered, a send precedes its receive, and the relation is transitive. Events not related are concurrent.

first_principles.problem: Replicas apply updates in different orders and diverge, despite synchronised clocks.
truths: Causality matters more than wall time.

analogy.title: Email reply chains
analogy.story: You know a reply came after the original, even without timestamps, because it quotes it.
analogy.breaks: Emails are human-readable; logical clocks are numbers that must be propagated correctly.

example.title: Happened-before
flow: P3's event d unrelated → concurrent with all
example.outcome: causality as the foundation of ordering.

check.q: When are two events 'concurrent' in Lamport's model?

lamport-timestamps-the-simple-counter.core: A Lamport clock is a counter per process: increment before each event, attach it to messages, and on receive set counter = max(local, received) + 1. If A → B then L(A) < L(B), giving a total order (with process ID tie-breaks) consistent with causality. The converse doesn't hold: L(A) < L(B) doesn't mean A caused B.

first_principles.problem: A distributed mutual exclusion scheme needs a consistent global order of requests.
derivation: **Tie-break** by process ID for total order.

analogy.title: Ticket numbers that always increase when you hear about a higher one
analogy.story: You always take a number higher than any you've seen.
analogy.breaks: Ticket numbers are unique per shop; Lamport timestamps can collide across processes without tie-breaks.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Causally consistent ordering with one integer.

check.q: If L(A) < L(B), can you conclude A happened before B?
check.a: No; Lamport clocks only guarantee the reverse implication.

vector-clocks-detecting-concurrency.core: A vector clock keeps one counter per process. Each process increments its own entry on events and merges (element-wise max) on receive. Comparing vectors tells you whether A → B (all entries ≤, at least one <), B → A, or they're concurrent (neither dominates). Used for conflict detection in Dynamo-style stores and CRDTs, at the cost of size growing with participants.

first_principles.problem: Two clients update the same shopping cart on different replicas, and the system must detect the conflict rather than silently dropping one.
truths: Per-process counters capture full causal history.
Size grows with number of writers.

analogy.title: Each friend tracking how many messages they've seen from everyone
analogy.story: Comparing tallies reveals whether one person had seen the other's news before replying.
analogy.breaks: Friends' tallies stay small; vectors grow with every client or replica.

example.title: Detecting concurrency
flow: Neither dominates → concurrent → keep both siblings or merge

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Conflict surfaced instead of lost update.

check.q: How do you know two vector clocks represent concurrent events?
check.a: Neither vector is less than or equal to the other in every entry.

google-truetime-the-hybrid-solution.core: Google's TrueTime (used by Spanner) uses GPS and atomic clocks in every datacenter to return an interval [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain true time, with uncertainty ε of a few milliseconds. Spanner assigns commit timestamps and then waits out the uncertainty (commit wait) so timestamps order transactions globally (external consistency). Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) offer a cheaper approximation used by CockroachDB.

first_principles.problem: A globally distributed database needs transaction order matching real time without central coordination.
truths: Bounded uncertainty is better than unknown uncertainty.
Waiting out uncertainty gives ordering guarantees.

analogy.title: Two people agreeing who arrived first by waiting out their watch error
analogy.story: If watches can be off by 5 ms, wait 5 ms before declaring your arrival time final.
analogy.breaks: People can't wait for every arrival; Spanner waits milliseconds per commit, which is acceptable.

example.title: Commit wait
flow: Commit visible; any later transaction gets a higher timestamp

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Global ordering consistent with real time.

check.q: What does Spanner's commit wait achieve?
check.a: It ensures a transaction's timestamp is in the past everywhere before it's visible, so timestamp order matches real-time order.
